title: Find Right Interval
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every interval per query versus pre-sorting starts once and binary searching each query.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of intervals, where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], find, for each interval i, the SMALLEST index j (the "right interval") such that start_j is greater than or equal to end_i, and start_j is the minimum such start among all qualifying intervals. Return -1 for interval i if no such interval exists.

blocks.text: For each interval, the task is to find another interval (by original index) whose start is at least this interval's end, and among all such candidates, the one with the smallest start. This is exactly a "find the ceiling" binary search query, repeated once per interval.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Next Available Appointment Slot
blocks.text: Picture a set of appointment slots, each with its own start and end time, and for every slot, wanting to know the NEXT slot (by index) that starts at or after this one ends, specifically the one starting as early as possible among all valid candidates. Sorting all start times once lets each of these lookups be answered quickly.

blocks.caption: Sorting (start, original index) pairs once enables a binary search "ceiling" query for every interval

blocks.text: Result: [-1, 0, 1]. Interval 0 ([3,4]) has no interval starting at 4 or later (-1). Interval 1 ([2,3]) matches interval 0 ([3,4], start 3 >= 3). Interval 2 ([1,2]) matches interval 1 ([2,3], start 2 >= 2).

Before scanning all other intervals for every query, notice that the query itself ("smallest start >= end_i") is a classic binary search "ceiling" lookup, so pre-sorting all start values ONCE (paired with their original indices) lets every interval's query be answered in O(log n) instead of O(n).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since start values are guaranteed distinct, sorting (start, original index) pairs by start gives a clean, well-defined ordering to binary search against.

Observation 2: For each interval i, the query "smallest start >= end_i" is a standard binary search for the leftmost position in the sorted starts array whose value is at least end_i.

Observation 3: If such a position exists, the paired original index at that position is the answer for interval i; if the binary search exhausts the array without finding one, the answer is -1.

Observation 4: Since sorting happens once (O(n log n)) and each of the n queries costs O(log n), the total cost is O(n log n), a significant improvement over checking every pair.
This leads to sorting (start, original index) pairs once, then for each interval, binary searching this sorted list for the smallest start >= that interval's end.
For each interval, scan every other interval directly, tracking the smallest qualifying start and its index.

items: For each interval i, scan every interval j.
If intervals[j][0] is >= intervals[i][1], track it as a candidate, keeping the one with the smallest start.
Record the best candidate's index (or -1 if none qualify) as the answer for interval i.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning every interval per query is wasteful: the query "find the smallest start >= X" is answerable via binary search if the starts are sorted, avoiding the need to re-scan for every single query.

The pre-sort trick: sort (start, original index) pairs by start ONCE, in O(n log n); this sorted list can then be binary searched for EVERY interval's query.

Answering each query: for interval i, binary search this sorted list for the leftmost entry with start >= intervals[i][1] (a standard "ceiling" binary search); the paired original index there is the answer, or -1 if none exists.

The core idea: sort once, then binary search per query, replacing n separate O(n) scans with n separate O(log n) lookups against one pre-sorted structure.

Sort (start, original index) pairs by start. For each interval, binary search this sorted list for the smallest start >= its end; the paired original index is the answer, or -1 if the search finds nothing.

blocks.caption: Binary search the pre-sorted starts list for each interval's "ceiling" query

codes.python:
import bisect

def find_right_interval(intervals):
    n = len(intervals)
    starts = sorted((intervals[i][0], i) for i in range(n))    # sort once
    start_values = [s[0] for s in starts]
    result = [-1] * n
    for i in range(n):
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(start_values, intervals[i][1])   # binary search per query
        if idx < n:
            result[i] = starts[idx][1]
    return result

blocks.text: Sorting (start, original index) pairs once creates a structure that directly supports the "smallest start >= X" query via binary search: the leftmost position where start is at least the queried end value is exactly the ceiling, and its paired original index correctly identifies which interval that corresponds to. Since this sorted structure is built only once and reused for all n queries, the total cost drops from O(n squared) to O(n log n).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), for the sort plus n binary searches.
Space: O(n) for the sorted starts array and result.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Scanning every interval per query costs O(n squared) time; pre-sorting starts once and binary searching per query costs O(n log n) time, both using O(n) space.

items: Pattern: pre-sort once, then binary search per query, a widely reusable technique for answering many similar range queries efficiently.
Core Idea: sort (start, original index) pairs by start; for each interval, binary search this sorted list for the smallest start >= its end.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: pre-sorting once amortizes the cost across all n queries, turning O(n) per-query scans into O(log n) per-query binary searches.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, well-known application of "sort once, binary search many" beyond a single lookup.
One line memory trick: sort (start, index) pairs once; binary search each interval's end against them.
